Of the solution-update time, applying the streamed projects, configurations and files to the database.

Of those, answered from the context's file cache.

Time spent building per-file compilation configurations during walks.
Of the build-configs time, walking the project (the half that is the same for every file of a project, and is cached).
Of the build-configs time, reaching each file's own configuration.
Of the build-configs time, reading the per-file properties.

Of the build-configs time, resolving each configuration's include lists to existing absolute directories. The four do not add up to the total - the remainder is the work around them (IPC conversion, cloning the cached entry).
Per-file configuration derivations requested during walks.
Of those lookups, how many the project-level cache answered without redoing the project half.
Include lists sanitized during walks - up to three per file.
Of those, how many the sanitize memo answered without re-checking every directory on disk. A low share means the per-file include lists keep changing, so each miss stats the whole list again.
Directories the sanitize misses actually checked on disk.
Directories answered from the directory cache instead. Include lists that differ per file still name the same directories over and over, which is what this collapses.
Of the file-properties time, evaluating a makefile project's own .vcxproj. Once per project and configuration, not per file.
Of the file-properties time, reading each file's settings out of that project - the load above included.
Of the file-properties time, merging those per-file settings into the configuration. Grows with the size of the list already collected.
Of the collect-files time, reading each item's child list - this is what realizes the project's virtual folders.
Of the collect-files time, asking each item for its file path and checking that path on disk.
Project items the walk touched, across every project. Collect-files time minus build-configs, item enumeration and item probe is the remainder (config dedup and list building).

Of those, the ones that became project items - the rest are folders, non-source extensions, or paths that are not on disk. Visited staying near collected means a project's files were never handed to the walk at all.
Files parsed by clang-tidy this session.

Of the parse time, launching this item's own child clang process (the first call to it is what spawns it) and taking hold of it. Until that is done the child runs at the server's own OS priority, so this is also parsing that the low-priority setting did not apply to.
Of child start, the call that actually launches the child process and waits for clang to come up on it.
Of child start, resolving the child's process id and setting its OS priority.
Of the parse time, composing the compilation options - every include and source path is normalized - and constructing the parser on the child.
Of the parse time, clang actually parsing the file. This is the only part that is compilation work; a big gap between this and the parse total is per-item process overhead.

Of the parse time, destroying the parser on the child. Expected to be 0: the parser is left for the child process exit to reclaim, since it is stopped immediately afterwards. A pooled child, which outlives the parse, would have to destroy it for real.
Of the parse time, fetching the cleaned-up replacements for fixes that need them, which has to happen while the child is still alive.
Of the parse time, tearing the child down: asking it to quit, a bounded wait for it to go, and deleting its temp directory.
Of child stop, asking the child to quit.
Of child stop, the bounded wait for the child process to actually go, so its temp directory can be deleted.
Of child stop, deleting the child's temp directory - retried, because clang can still hold a file in it.
Times a finished parse's results and fixes were written to the database - the "storing results" phase of a parse task.
Total time storing parse results and fixes to the database.
Average time to store one parse's results (includes waiting for the database write lock).
Of the result-store time, the part actually holding the database write lock. The rest is waiting to get in. Only this part costs wall clock - it is what other tasks are blocked behind.
Of the store hold, deleting the item's previous parse results.
Of the store hold, the EF flush that writes the sketch and its fixes.
Recording which editor buffers the stored results reflect - its own write-lock acquisition, made right after the store.
Of the stores, how many deflated the parse's debug output (clang-tidy's fixes-YAML export and its console text) on the way into the database. One per store, covering both blobs.
Total time deflating those blobs. Part of the result-store time above, but spent BEFORE the database write lock is taken - so unlike the rest of a store it makes no other parse wait.

What that debug output would have taken in the database stored as text. It is the same diagnostics the Fixes table already holds, kept verbatim for the dbBrowser tab, and it used to be nearly the whole database.
What it actually took after deflating.

Parses that failed with an exception (crash/timeout counted separately).

Of the deps-update time, the part with the database write lock actually held - the work that makes other tasks wait.

Reading the item's stored include dependencies (and their file rows) that the diff runs against. Part of "lock held".
Re-stating every dependency's file on disk, so the next solution walk does not see them as changed. Part of "lock held".
Dependency files the scan actually stat'd. Counted per dependency edge, so a header included by many items can be counted many times.
Dependency edges the scan skipped because the file's disk state was already known from an earlier parse. Skipped plus stat'd is the total edge count.
Persisting the dependency diff (inserts/removals). Part of "lock held".

Database sections of a parse task outside every phase above: marking the item Processing and resolving its configuration on the way in, then clearing or re-queueing it on the way out. Two per task, so this counts sections, not tasks.
Total time in those sections, including waiting for the database write lock.
Average time per section (not per task).
Of that, the part actually holding the database write lock, summed over both sections. A large gap to the total above means the sections are queueing, not working.
Times the database write lock was taken, from any thread. Most are uncontended, so this is closer to "how much database traffic" than to "how often something waited".

Total time BLOCKED on the database write lock before any database work started - contention, not database work. Already included in the phase timings above (result store, deps update, db update), so do not add it to them.
Waiting time divided by acquisitions. Diluted by the uncontended ones - read the total for how much waiting there actually was.

Time the write lock was HELD, across every acquisition from any thread. Compare it with the scan's elapsed time: if they are close the lock is saturated and the scan is bound by serialized database work, so removing work from any single caller only redistributes the waiting.
